experiments.title: GPU flow field
experiments.summary: The hero's flow field runs on the GPU (WebGPU compute shader) instead of WebAssembly, so it can draw fifty to a hundred times as many particles.
experiments.measure: Holds 60 fps from 3,000 to 1,000,000 particles on an Apple GPU (Metal); the WebAssembly field reaches its limit near 150,000. At the site's own density there is no gain, which is why it is off by default.

experiments.title: Hero of the day
experiments.summary: The hero's flow field is a different picture each UTC day: the noise field moves to a new place and the particles start somewhere new. The same seed draws the same field on the WebAssembly and GPU paths.
experiments.measure: Not yet judged. A seed of 0 is the field the site has always drawn, so with the switch off nothing changes. Add ?seed=anything to any visit to pin one picture, for example /?seed=flow.

experiments.title: HDR glow for the GPU field
experiments.summary: On a display that can show it, the GPU field draws into a floating-point canvas with extended tone mapping, so where trails pile up they glow brighter than the page's white. Works together with the GPU field; on any other display nothing changes.
experiments.measure: Not yet judged: the glow has to be looked at on an HDR screen, and automated tests only check that the browser accepts it and falls back cleanly. Try it with the GPU field and a dense field: /?lab=hero-gpu,hero-hdr&particles=60000.

experiments.title: View as agent
experiments.summary: A button on every page that shows what a crawler or an AI agent gets there: the page as Markdown (Cloudflare converts it at the edge, with a token estimate), the read-only tools on the MCP server, and the documents agents start from.
experiments.measure: Not yet judged. It has to work on the home page, a project and a post, and must never leave Markdown cached under a page's address: the service worker skips any request that asks for Markdown (a unit test) and the fetch bypasses the browser cache.

experiments.title: Shared flow field
experiments.summary: Everyone who has this switched on bends the same hero: move the pointer over it and the field moves for the other visitors who have it on, and theirs moves yours. Only a coarse pointer position is sent, only while at least two people have it on, nothing is stored, and nobody is named. It needs someone else to be here at the same time.
experiments.measure: Not yet judged. Two browsers should see each other within about 150 ms, a day of use should add no visible Durable Object cost, and the object must still hibernate when nobody is moving. Dropped if cost or abuse limits get complicated. At most 25 pages take part at once.

experiments.title: Post tools, on your device
experiments.summary: On a post, two buttons that use the model built into the browser: key points, and the post read in Spanish, French, German or Japanese. Nothing is sent anywhere, the first use downloads a large model, and the result says it was made by the model and the post is the source.
experiments.measure: Not yet judged. Only desktop Chrome and Edge have these APIs, and they need a lot of disk and a capable GPU, so most visitors will see nothing. Kept only if the key points of the posts are accurate; a post too long for the model is not summarised rather than cut short.
